note: Row-count assertions, not smoke tests. On Databend a mistranslated query returns zero rows and raises no error, so 'the SQL executed' proves nothing. Every case here states a relationship between two counts. Baselines are relative, so the suite stays valid as the table grows.

cases.name: empty search returns everything
cases.note: The whole reason this project exists. match(msg,'') returns 0 rows silently, and the optimiser pushes match() into the index scan regardless of the surrounding boolean, so an empty box must compile to SQL containing no match() at all.

cases.name: AND narrows
cases.note: Adjacency means AND, so adding a term can only shrink the result set. If this ever exceeds the baseline, the default operator has silently become OR. The pair must be one that genuinely co-occurs: with disjoint terms the intersection is legitimately 0, and 0 passes any upper-bound assertion — so this uses `narrows`, which also requires the count to be nonzero. Co-occurrence alone is not enough either — it has to be abundant. An earlier version of this case paired two terms that met in five rows out of half a million, all of them written by one process inside a two-millisecond window: the case passed, but it sat one retention boundary away from failing for a reason that had nothing to do with the compiler.

cases.name: phrase is order-sensitive
cases.note: Positions are stored: 72,601 rows for this phrase against 0 for the reversed one when measured.

cases.name: reversed phrase finds nothing
cases.note: Negative control for the case above. If this is ever nonzero, phrase search has degenerated to an unordered token AND.

cases.name: fuzzy typo matches the baseline
cases.note: The headline fix. Typed as Lucene `snapshoot~1` this returns 0 through query(); compiled to match(msg,'snapshoot','fuzziness=1') it returns the baseline and a little more (measured 17,341 against 17,336) because other tokens also sit within one edit of the stem. Hence 'at least the baseline', not equality.

cases.name: fuzziness is bounded
cases.note: Two edits from the stem, rejected at fuzziness=1. Guards against fuzzy matching degenerating into match-anything. NOTE: edit distance is measured against the STEM, not the typed word.

cases.name: two edits accepted at fuzziness 2
cases.note: Measured 17,321 against a 17,316 baseline: fuzziness=2 matches a few extra tokens, so the assertion is 'at least the baseline', not equality.

cases.name: prefix wildcard works via LIKE
cases.note: Through query() the star is silently ignored and `snapsh*` returns 0 while `snapshot*` returns the full baseline, which looks like success. Compiled to LIKE 'snapsh%' it returns real rows.

cases.name: negation excludes
cases.note: MUST-VERIFY. Negating a match() relies on the optimiser handling an inverted-index scan under NOT. §5.1 showed match() pushdown does not always respect the surrounding boolean, so this is the case most likely to expose an engine bug rather than a compiler bug. Asserted as an exact partition of the baseline rather than an upper bound, because NOT swallowing the whole predicate yields 0, which is also <= the baseline. `partitions` only means something while both halves are non-empty, so the pair is chosen for a large intersection rather than a merely non-zero one.

cases.name: negation of an absent term changes nothing
cases.note: Sharper than the case above: excluding a term that matches nothing must leave the count untouched. If this comes back 0, NOT is swallowing the whole predicate.

cases.name: structured filter is case-insensitive
cases.note: There is no case-insensitive `=` on this engine, so case-insensitivity is compiled explicitly with lower() on both sides. ILIKE does exist - measured, `pod ILIKE '%tikv%'` and `lower(pod) LIKE lower('%tikv%')` return the same 189,623 rows - but it is a LIKE, so using it for equality would turn `component:tikv` into a substring match.

cases.name: hyphen is not negation
cases.note: Pod names carry hyphens; if `-` were treated as an operator inside a word the predicate would silently invert.

cases.name: quote in a term does not break the literal
cases.note: Injection safety. The assertion is parseability, not a count: `it's` compiles to a phrase search that legitimately matches (2,056 rows measured, since the tokenizer splits on the apostrophe). What must never happen is a syntax error or a broken string literal.

cases.name: literal percent is not a wildcard
cases.note: Verifies the two layers of escaping: LIKE's backslash-percent keeps the percent literal, and the SQL literal doubles the backslash. If Databend does NOT honour backslash escapes inside string literals this case will misbehave — that is exactly what it is here to detect.

cases.name: boolean AND agrees with LIKE
cases.note: Both terms merge into one query() call. Two match() calls would fail [1065] duplicate search function.

cases.name: negation subtracts exactly
cases.note: The name is now the assertion: `peer -status` plus `peer status` must equal `peer` exactly, no rows lost or double-counted. Measured 21,418 + 74,207 = 95,625.

cases.name: fuzzy composes with a structured filter
cases.note: match(...,'fuzziness=1') is the one search function; the column predicate is not one, so they compose.

cases.name: fuzzy composes with LIKE
cases.note: LIKE is not a search function either, so a rewritten fuzzy term and a rewritten wildcard coexist in one statement without tripping the one-search-function rule. The two halves have to land on the same rows for this to assert anything, which is why both are drawn from a message shape the cluster is still emitting.

cases.name: field-scoped group partitions the table
cases.note: A field in front of a group used to be dropped along with the group, compiling to 1=1 - a filter that silently matches everything, which is the exact failure this project exists to eliminate. An upper bound would not catch it, because 1=1 returns the baseline. This one does, twice over: the positive half has to be strictly smaller than the table AND the negated half has to be non-empty, and a dropped filter makes the negated half zero. Measured 98,623 + 351,270 = 449,893.

cases.name: a field-scoped group means OR, not AND
cases.note: Sharper than the partition above on one specific way to get grouping wrong. If the OR inside the group were silently read as the default AND, the count would collapse to the rows that are somehow both ERROR and WARN, which is none. Measured 98,623 against 89,336.

cases.name: a field-scoped group on the text column stays one search function
cases.note: The real assertion is that this statement runs at all. Grouping on the full-text column must fold into a single query() call - emitting one search function per branch would fail [1065] duplicate search function for table 0, and the harness would report a failure rather than a count. Measured 125,241 against 109,950.

cases.name: OR with a negation folds through De Morgan
cases.note: This shape used to be a compile error, because `(a) OR NOT (b)` drops the negative clause silently on this engine. De Morgan rewrites it into the clause shape that works. Scoping it under a third term keeps all three predicates inside a single query() call, which matters twice over: it is the composed form, where the fold sits nested inside another negative group, and it keeps every side of the identity on the same side of the index-scan boundary. `c AND (a OR NOT b)` and `c AND b AND NOT a` tile `c` exactly. Measured 15,634 + 4,510 = 20,144.

cases.name: OR with a negation does not quietly mean the positive half
cases.note: The failure the old compile error described: the engine drops the negative clause from `(a) OR NOT (b)` and the search quietly means `a`. If the De Morgan fold ever regresses to that, this count collapses to exactly the baseline. Measured 523,451 against 112,661. Note the whole-table complement is NOT assertable here - `NOT (query(...))` sees only the blocks the index scan visits, so a partition against the row count of the table is off by however many rows were ingested since the index last caught up.

cases.name: the required-term marker is consumed, not searched for
cases.note: Lucene's `+` means required, and adjacency already means AND here, so `+a +b` and `a b` must be the same search. The marker used to be left in the search text, where it became `query('(msg:"+peer") AND (msg:"+status")')` - a phrase query for a token the tokenizer happens to strip, so the count came out right by luck. It does not come out right on a plain string column, where there is no tokenizer to save it, and a phrase query is not what was asked for either.

cases.name: a dotted path reaches the bag key
cases.note: Naming the VARIANT column explicitly must reach the same key as leaving it off. The whole dotted name used to be used as one flat key, kv['kv.container'], which no row has. Measured 6,742 both ways.

cases.name: negation includes the rows that lack the key
cases.note: Three-valued logic, and the reason negation is compiled as COALESCE(NOT (...), TRUE) rather than a bare NOT. `NOT (col = 'x')` is NULL - and therefore excluded - wherever the key is absent, so the positive and negative halves of the same term did not add up to the table: 6,742 + 443,148 = 449,890, three rows short. Every column here is nullable and 97% of rows carry no key beyond the common ones, so this is live behaviour rather than a hypothetical. Measured after the fix: 6,742 + 443,151 = 449,893.

cases.name: a colon inside a URL is not a field selector
cases.note: The URL used to compile to a lookup of a field named http, land in the VARIANT bag and return nothing, with a warning that read as though the user had asked for a field. The baseline is the same text as a wildcard, which cannot be misread as a field because a leading star is not a legal field name - so the two must agree exactly. Measured 50 both ways. The rule applies to every colon in the query, not just the first.

cases.name: a bracket range partitions on the timestamp
cases.note: Two-sided bracket ranges are plain SQL comparisons, never the search mini-language: query('msg:[a TO b]') fails with [1903] Unsupported query, Range query boundary cannot have multiple tokens. The exclusive and inclusive halves either side of one instant must tile the table exactly, which is what pins the boundary handling - an off-by-one on inclusivity would double-count or drop the rows at the boundary.

cases.name: an inclusive bracket range is the two one-sided terms
cases.note: `field:[a TO b]` must mean exactly what the two one-sided terms already meant. Before bracket ranges existed this mis-parsed into three bogus full-text terms - a search for `[2026-08-18`, `TO` and `2026-08-19]` - and returned nothing, so eq with a non-empty baseline is what catches the regression. Deliberately not routed through the search mini-language: query('msg:[a TO b]') fails with [1903] Unsupported query, Range query boundary cannot have multiple tokens. The bounds are a typed column rather than a bag key on purpose - a range over a VARIANT key casts every value in the table and hard-fails the whole statement the moment one row's value is not numeric, which is a live hazard here.

cases.name: a time-of-day bound is not truncated at the colon
cases.note: The nastiest class on this surface, because it does not look broken. The lexer used to split on every colon, so the bound became '2026-08-18T22' - which Databend accepts without complaint and resolves to 22:00:00, silently widening the window by up to an hour. Both bounds truncated to the same literal, so the two counts were equal and any upper-bound assertion passed. Strict inequality is what catches it. Measured 70,681 against 129,009.

cases.name: a regex is narrower than the unordered AND
cases.note: Regex compiles to RLIKE, which is not a search function and so composes with the single query() call, at the cost of a full scan - no index serves it. Requiring peer before status can only match a subset of the rows containing both. Also worth knowing: RLIKE is case-insensitive on this engine whatever the schema says, and (?-i) is how a pattern asks for case sensitivity.

cases.name: boost changes ranking, not the result set
cases.note: A relevance weight is a ranking device: it reorders score() and leaves the matched set alone. If these two ever diverge, the boost has been compiled into something that filters. Measured 125,241 both ways.

cases.name: excluding a term that occurs nowhere returns everything
cases.note: The defect this replaced was shipped and silent. `NOT (query(x))` is not the complement of `query(x)`: the search function is pushed into the index scan whatever the surrounding boolean, so when x matches no row the scan is pruned and the NOT returns ZERO rows instead of every row. Measured over a 152,317-row window, three absent tokens - zzzznosuchtoken, qqqqwwww and pdctl - each returned 0 through the bare NOT and the full window through the anti-join this now emits. Excluding a noise pattern that happens not to occur in the selected time range is an ordinary thing to ask, and the answer used to be an empty screen. Note that case 13 does NOT cover this: there the exclusion sits inside one query() call, where a positive term drives the scan.

cases.name: excluding a term that does occur partitions the table
cases.note: The control for the case above: with a token that is present, the exclusion must still be an exact complement rather than merely non-empty. Measured 353,902 + 95,991 = 449,893 in a frozen window, and 456,047 + 97,833 = 553,880 live. This one is assertable at whole-table scale where the same identity through a bare NOT is not, because the anti-join leaves the outer scan free of a search function - so the outer scan sees every row, including the most recent hour of ingest that the inverted index has not caught up on.

cases.name: OR with a negation survives an exclusion that matches nothing
cases.note: The De Morgan fold's own version of the case above, and the reason the fold could not ship on a bare NOT. `a OR -b` becomes the complement of `b AND NOT a`, and that inner expression matches nothing whenever b does not occur - or, less obviously, whenever every b also matches a. Through a bare NOT the whole search would then return 0 rows, silently, where the honest answer is every row: `-b` is vacuously true, so `a OR -b` is true everywhere.

cases.name: proximity widens the exact phrase
cases.note: Phrase proximity is real on this engine and N is honoured. The full ladder, frozen: "region peer" 654, ~0 654, ~1 654, ~2 4,593, ~3 4,593, ~10 4,853, and the unordered AND 4,853 - strictly monotone, converging on the AND. It is easy to measure this wrongly: sample only the exact phrase and a large N and both land on plateaus, which reads as N being ignored. An earlier revision of this library rejected the marker at compile time on exactly that mistake.

cases.name: proximity is bounded above by the unordered AND
cases.note: The other end of the ladder. However far the slop is opened it can never match more than the two tokens co-occurring anywhere in the line, so a slop phrase that ever exceeds the plain AND has stopped being a phrase. Measured 4,853 against 4,853 - equal at this N, which narrows permits while still requiring both to be non-empty.

cases.name: proximity below the transposition cost finds nothing
cases.note: A reversed phrase is a transposition, which costs two, so at ~1 it must still find nothing while the forward phrase finds many. If this ever goes non-zero the slop has stopped being a distance and become an unordered AND - the exact behaviour an earlier measurement wrongly attributed to this engine.

cases.name: proximity at the transposition cost finds the reversed phrase
cases.note: One more than the case above, and the reversed phrase matches - exactly the forward phrase's rows, 88,441 both ways, because every co-occurrence here is adjacent. Together the two cases pin N to a real edit distance rather than an on/off switch.
